# Gynecomastia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Family medicine > Endocrine and metabolic disorders > Gynecomastia*

[Original Article Link](/library/M70Mmh)

---

## Summary

Gynecomastia is the <u>proliferation</u> of <u>mammary gland</u> tissue in male individuals, including those with <u>Klinefelter syndrome</u>; <u>neonatal gynecomastia</u> manifests in both male and female <u>infants</u>. Gynecomastia is caused by an increased <u>estrogen</u>/<u>testosterone</u> <u>ratio</u> that can be physiological (typically in <u>neonates</u>, during <u>puberty</u>, or in older adults), pathological (e.g., due to medications, <u>liver cirrhosis</u>, <u>chronic kidney disease</u>, <u>estrogen</u>-secreting tumors), or <u>idiopathic</u>. Gynecomastia is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> confirmed by identifying palpable <u>glandular tissue</u> on <u>physical examination</u>. A <u>medication review</u> should be performed in all patients; <u>drug-induced gynecomastia</u> accounts for 25% of cases. Diagnostics are not routinely recommended for individuals with <u>physiological gynecomastia</u>. <u>Breast</u> imaging may be considered to rule out differential diagnoses or if <u>physical examination</u> findings are inconclusive. Diagnostic workup for <u>pathological gynecomastia</u> should be guided by clinical evaluation and includes <u>laboratory studies</u> to evaluate for chronic diseases (e.g., <u>liver chemistries</u>, <u>renal function tests</u>, <u>thyroid function tests</u>), <u>hypogonadism</u> (e.g., <u>sex hormone profile</u>), or <u>malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>tumor markers</u>, imaging, <u>biopsy</u>). <u>Pathological gynecomastia</u> can usually be managed by treating the underlying cause. <u>Physiological gynecomastia</u> usually regresses spontaneously. <u>Surgery</u> (e.g., <u>nipple-sparing mastectomy</u>) may be considered for <u>pathological gynecomastia</u> unresponsive to treatment of the underlying cause, longstanding gynecomastia, or cosmesis.

---

## Etiology

Gynecomastia is caused by an increased <u>estrogen</u>/<u>testosterone</u> <u>ratio</u> (e.g., elevated <u>estrogen</u> levels, decreased <u>testosterone</u> levels, or both) but can be <u>idiopathic</u> in upto 25% of patients. It is the most common abnormality of the male <u>breast</u>. [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[3]](/library/eo0xaS)[[4]](/library/xWYEnL)




### Physiological gynecomastia [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




* Neonatal gynecomastia [[5]](/library/EWY8ML)

* Occurs in ∼ 90% of <u>neonates</u> due to <u>placental</u> transfer of maternal <u>estrogens</u>

* Gynecomastia is bilateral, sex independent, and spontaneously resolves within a few weeks or months.

* Pubertal gynecomastia [[6]](/library/CWYqnL)

* Occurs in ∼ 50% of <u>adolescent</u> boys (typically occurs in patients aged 10–14 years)

* Caused by pubertal <u>estrogen</u>/<u>androgen</u> imbalance

* Clinical features

* Small, mobile, firm <u>plaques</u> of <u>breast</u> tissue in the subareolar region that develop during <u>puberty</u>

* Can be tender, unilateral/bilateral, and associated with fatty development around the <u>nipple</u>

* Spontaneously resolves (usually by 17 years of age)

* Pharmacotherapy or <u>surgery</u> can be considered for persistent <u>pubertal gynecomastia</u> or if symptoms cause significant <u>distress</u>.

* Senile gynecomastia: occurs in ∼ 50% of men > 50 years





### Pathological gynecomastia [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




#### Due to <u>estrogen</u> excess




* Malignancies

* <u>Leydig cell tumor</u>

* <u>Sertoli cell tumor</u>

* <u>Ectopic</u> <u>hCG</u>-producing tumors (e.g., <u>lung cancer</u>, <u>hepatocellular carcinoma</u>)

* Adrenocortical tumors

* <u>Liver cirrhosis</u>: due to increased conversion of <u>adrenal</u> <u>androgen</u> precursors to <u>estrogen</u>

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u>: due to

* ↑ peripheral conversion of <u>androgens</u> to <u>estrogens</u>

* ↑ hepatic production of <u>sex hormone binding globulin</u> (<u>SHBG</u>), which has a higher affinity for <u>testosterone</u> → ↓ free <u>testosterone</u> and a relative increase in <u>estrogen</u> [[7]](/library/rPXfTy)

* Refeeding (after prolonged <u>starvation</u>)  [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)





#### Due to decreased <u>testosterone</u>




* <u>Klinefelter syndrome</u>

* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>  [[8]](/library/HPXKTy)

* Testicular disorders (e.g., <u>mumps orchitis</u>, castration, trauma to both <u>testes</u>)

* <u>Hypogonadism</u>

* <u>Hyperprolactinemia</u>  [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)

* <u>Starvation</u>





#### Drug-induced [[10]](/library/HI1KVR0)[[11]](/library/_WY5LL)




Drug-induced gynecomastia accounts for up to 25% of cases. [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[10]](/library/HI1KVR0)




* Inhibitors of <u>testosterone</u> <u>receptors</u>

* <u>Antiandrogens</u>;  (e.g., <u>finasteride</u>, <u>bicalutamide</u>, <u>cyproterone acetate</u>, <u>flutamide</u>)

* High-dose <u>cimetidine</u> (<u>H<sub>2</sub> receptor blocker</u>)

* <u>Spironolactone</u>

* Inhibitors of <u>testosterone</u> synthesis

* <u>Ketoconazole</u>

* <u>Spironolactone</u>

* <u>Chemotherapy drugs</u> (e.g., <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>methotrexate</u>, <u>bleomycin</u>, <u>cisplatin</u>, <u>vincristine</u>)

* <u>Exogenous</u> <u>androgens</u> and <u>androgenic steroids</u> ;  [[12]](/library/vWYAML)

* <u>Exogenous</u> <u>testosterone</u>

* <u>Androgen</u> precursors (e.g., <u>DHEA</u>, <u>androstenedione</u>)

* <u>Androgenic steroids</u>

* <u>Estrogen</u> <u>receptor</u> stimulators

* <u>Estrogens</u>

* <u>Digitalis</u> compounds

* <u>Marijuana</u>

* <u>Opioids</u>

* <u>cART</u> drugs





> [!NOTE]
> Some Hormones Cause Fulminant Kleavage: Spironolactone, Hormones, Cimetidine, Finasteride, Ketoconazole cause gynecomastia.

---

## Clinical features

* Firm, concentric, typically mobile mass in the subareolar region

* May be tender

* Typically bilateral

* In <u>pathological gynecomastia</u>: possible features of undervirilization, <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>liver</u>/<u>kidney</u> disease, etc.

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




* Obtain a detailed <u>medical history</u> (including a <u>medication review</u>; see <u>drug-induced gynecomastia</u>).

* Perform a thorough <u>physical examination</u>.

* Confirm gynecomastia (i.e., palpable glandular <u>breast</u> tissue) on <u>physical examination</u>.

* Distinguish between physiological and <u>pathological gynecomastia</u> based on clinical evaluation.

* <u>Physiological gynecomastia</u> likely: Diagnostic workup is not routinely recommended.

* Suspected <u>pathological gynecomastia</u> or symptom onset in adulthood: Evaluate for an underlying etiology; consider specialist (e.g., <u>endocrinology</u>) referral.





> [!WARNING]
> Examine <u>the breasts</u> and <u>testes</u> in all patients with gynecomastia. Expedite further diagnostics (e.g., imaging, <u>biopsies</u>) if <u>malignancy</u> is suspected (e.g., features of <u>breast cancer</u>; testicular mass on palpation or imaging). [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)




> [!TIP]
> Assess all patients with symptom onset in adulthood for <u>pathological gynecomastia</u>, even when an apparent cause has been identified. [[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




#### Routine studies  [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




* <u>Liver chemistries</u>

* <u>Urea</u> and <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>





#### Suspected <u>hypogonadism</u>




* <u>Sex hormone profile</u>  [[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)

* ↑ <u>LH</u> (with ↓ or normal <u>testosterone</u>): <u>primary hypogonadism</u> [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)

* ↓ <u>LH</u> and ↑ <u>estradiol</u>: <u>testicular tumor</u>, <u>stress</u>, or <u>exogenous</u> <u>estrogen</u> [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[9]](/library/RP1leS0)

* ↓ <u>LH</u> and ↓ <u>testosterone</u>: <u>secondary hypogonadism</u> or <u>prolactinoma</u>

* Serum <u>prolactin</u> levels: Elevated levels are suggestive of <u>prolactinoma</u>.  [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[14]](/library/sI1tVR0)





#### Suspected <u>estrogen</u>-secreting tumors



* <u>Tumor markers</u>

* Elevated <u>hCG</u> or <u>alpha-fetoprotein</u>: suggestive of <u>testicular germ cell tumors</u>  [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)

* Elevated <u>dehydroepiandrosterone</u>: suggestive of <u>adrenal</u> tumors [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




> [!WARNING]
> Elevated <u>hCG</u>, <u>alpha-fetoprotein</u>, and/or <u>dehydroepiandrosterone</u> is suggestive of <u>malignancy</u>. [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




> [!TIP]
> If all laboratory tests are normal, including the <u>hormone</u> profile, gynecomastia is likely <u>idiopathic</u>. [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




### Imaging




#### <u>Breast</u> imaging [[15]](/library/MI1MWR0)




<u>Breast</u> imaging is not routinely recommended in patients with clinical features consistent with gynecomastia or <u>pseudogynecomastia</u>. [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[15]](/library/MI1MWR0)




* Indications and preferred first-line modalities

* Indeterminate <u>breast mass</u> on <u>physical examination</u>

* Age < 25 years: <u>ultrasound</u> <u>breast</u>

* Age ≥ 25 years: <u>mammography</u> or <u>digital breast tomosynthesis</u>

* <u>Examination findings concerning for breast cancer</u>: <u>mammography</u>, <u>digital breast tomosynthesis</u>, or <u>ultrasound</u> <u>breast</u>

* Supportive findings of gynecomastia [[15]](/library/MI1MWR0)[[16]](/library/KI1UdR0)

* On <u>ultrasound</u>: subareolar <u>hypoechoic</u> mass

* On <u>mammography</u>: normal <u>breast</u> tissue





> [!TIP]
> Consider routinely <u>screening for breast cancer</u> in all patients with <u>Klinefelter syndrome</u> who present with gynecomastia; these individuals have a significantly higher risk (16–30 times) of <u>breast cancer</u> than those with XY <u>chromosomes</u>. [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Breast</u> lesions concerning for <u>malignancy</u> on imaging or <u>physical examination</u> should be urgently biopsied (e.g., <u>core needle biopsy</u>). [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)




#### Testicular <u>ultrasound</u>




Some guidelines recommend testicular <u>ultrasound</u> for all individuals with gynecomastia; others recommend imaging only in the following cases:  [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




* Suspected <u>testicular tumor</u>  [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[14]](/library/sI1tVR0)

* Suspected <u>hypogonadism</u>  [[14]](/library/sI1tVR0)

* Gynecomastia > 5 cm [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)

* <u>Pathological gynecomastia</u> of unknown etiology [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)





#### <u>Neuroimaging</u> [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




* To evaluate for <u>pituitary adenoma</u> (e.g., in patients with elevated serum <u>prolactin</u> levels)

* See “<u>Diagnostics of pituitary adenoma</u>” for details.

---

## Treatment

### <u>Pathological gynecomastia</u> [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)




Treat the underlying cause and monitor for regression. Examples include:




* <u>Drug-induced gynecomastia</u>: If feasible, discontinue the causative agent.

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u>: See “<u>Treatment of hyperthyroidism</u>.”

* <u>Testicular tumor</u>: See “<u>Management of testicular cancer</u>.”

* Confirmed <u>hypogonadism</u>: <u>testosterone</u> replacement  [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)





> [!TIP]
> Most patients with gynecomastia experience spontaneous regression or respond well to management of the underlying condition. [[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




> [!TIP]
> After discontinuing medications or treating the underlying cause, an observation period is recommended to monitor for regression. <u>Surgery</u> can be considered for patients with persistent gynecomastia. [[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




### Physiological and <u>idiopathic</u> gynecomastia [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




<u>Watchful waiting</u> can be considered if no pathological cause is suspected and the patient is not disturbed by their symptoms.




* Reassurance and follow up every 6 months.  [[2]](/library/7PX4Ty)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)

* Provide adequate <u>analgesia</u>.

* Persistent gynecomastia

* Consider pharmacotherapy for persistent <u>pubertal gynecomastia</u> of recent onset.

* Consider <u>surgery</u> for long-standing gynecomastia and cosmesis.





### Pharmacotherapy [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




* Agents:  (<u>off-label</u>): <u>selective estrogen receptor modulators</u> (<u>tamoxifen</u>, <u>raloxifene</u>)

* Indications (limited evidence of benefit)

* Painful or persistent <u>pubertal gynecomastia</u> (duration < 2 years)  [[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)

* Treatment or prevention of gynecomastia secondary to <u>androgen</u> <u>ablation therapy</u> for <u>prostate cancer</u> (<u>tamoxifen</u> in particular)





### <u>Surgery</u> [[9]](/library/RP1leS0)[[13]](/library/3P1SeS0)




* Indications (not routinely required ; )

* Gynecomastia unresponsive to medical therapy or treatment of the underlying cause

* Long-standing symptomatic gynecomastia

* Cosmesis

* Examples 

* <u>Nipple</u>-sparing subcutaneous <u>mastectomy</u> ,

* Suction lipectomy
